title: Noah, Daniel, Job, and the Cedar
english: It seems, then, that he likens to Noah those who, through faith in God, serve him well; to Daniel, those who are wise and clear-sighted; and to Job, in turn, those who please him through endurance, clearly meaning endurance in anything at all that is praised.

“And I will take from the chosen parts of the cedar, from its top” (Ezekiel 17:22). He likens to cedars, tall and most beautiful, those who are from Israel. Among them the chosen part, and, as it were, a kind of heart, was the blessed David. From him God the Father took and planted Emmanuel, who also rose up into a great cedar and received all into his own shade (Ezekiel 17:23). And so, from then on, the whole world under the sun came to know the power and authority of God, who can do all things.
For he has brought low the green tree, and has made the dry tree grow and sprout again (Ezekiel 17:24), that is, the Church from among the Gentiles, which by the devil’s…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Fragmenta in Ezechielem (Greek), via the Khazarzar transcription.

Continues Cyril's comment on Ezekiel 14:14 from the previous section. The subject of ἔοικε ... παρεικάζειν is taken as the prophet ('he likens'); the Greek could also be read impersonally ('it is fitting to liken').

εὐεργετοῦντας αὐτῷ: literally 'doing good to him'; rendered 'serve him well'. The parallel εὐαρεστοῦντας αὐτῷ in the Job clause suggests a possible corruption, but the printed text is kept. 'Him' is God.
δῆλον δὲ ὅτι τῆς εἰς πᾶν ὁτιοῦν τῶν ἐπαινουμένων: Cyril widens Job's endurance to endurance in any praiseworthy thing; rendered 'clearly meaning endurance in anything at all that is praised'.

ἐν οἷς τὸ ἐπίλεκτον, καὶ οἱονεί τις καρδία γέγονεν ὁ μακάριος Δαβίδ: both 'the chosen part' and 'a kind of heart' are said of David. οἱονεί τις καρδία picks up καρδίας in the unquoted rest of Ezekiel 17:22 LXX ('from the top of their heart I will pluck').
ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατήρ: rendered 'God the Father'.
The great cedar that receives all into its shade takes up Ezekiel 17:23, where every bird rests under its shade.
τοῦ πάντα ἰσχύοντος Θεοῦ: 'God, who can do all things'.
Catena reference Cat. f. 208 is dropped from the reading text.
Ends mid-sentence: the dative noun πλεονεξίαις and the participle κατευανθέν stand at the start of the next section; the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing supplied.
baehrens: PG 70; Fragmenta in Ezechielem frag rem early

title: Ordinances That Were Not Good, and Greedy Shepherds
english: “And I gave them ordinances that were not good” (Ezekiel 20:25). For in so far as it bears on spiritual contemplation, the Law is holy, and the commandment is holy and just and good (Romans 7:12). But in so far as it concerns the futility of the practice itself, and worship in shadows alone, the ordinances are not good; indeed they do not even bring eternal life. For no one is justified by the Law, as it is written (Galatians 3:11).

“See, you eat up the milk” (Ezekiel 34:3). For while they demanded tithes, firstfruits, and thank offerings according to the Law, and reveled wantonly in the gifts the people brought, they took no account at all of the people’s salvation.
“Is it not enough for you that you grazed on the good pasture?” (Ezekiel 34:18). For those of the blood of Levi, being learned in the Law, and with, as it were, the finest pasture…
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Fragmenta in Ezechielem (Greek), via the Khazarzar transcription.
Opens mid-sentence, finishing the clause begun at the end of the previous section ('the Church from among the Gentiles, which by the devil's…'); the leading ellipsis marks the join.

κατευανθέν ita cod.: the editor marks the codex reading as doubtful ('so the manuscript'). κατευανθέω would mean 'bloom fully', which contradicts the dry tree; the sense requires καταυανθέν ('dried up, withered', from καταυαίνω), and 'withered' is rendered. The Latin editorial note is not carried into the reading text.
προστάγματα is rendered 'ordinances' throughout, to keep it apart from ἐντολή, 'commandment', in the Romans quotation.
τὴν τοῦ πράγματος εἰκαιότητα: 'the futility of the practice itself', that is, the bare letter of the rites as against their spiritual meaning.

τὴν ἐν σκιαῖς λατρείαν: 'worship in shadows'; possibly echoes Hebrews 8:5 and 10:1, but is Cyril's stock phrase and is left uncited. οὐδὲ ζωῆς τῆς αἰωνίου πρόξενα may look to the second half of Ezekiel 20:25 ('statutes by which they shall not live'); not cited.

οὐδένα τῆς σωτηρίας αὐτῶν ἐποιοῦντο λόγον: αὐτῶν most naturally refers to the people who brought the gifts (the flock neglected by the shepherds of Ezekiel 34), so the English says 'the people's salvation'. ἐκ λαῶν is rendered 'the people' because the plural here means the lay people of Israel, not the Gentile nations.
Catena references Cat. 210b, Cat. f. 224 and Cat. f. 224b are dropped from the reading text.

Ends mid-sentence: the participle ἔχοντες, which governs 'pasture' and 'water', and the main verb κατεπάτουν stand in the next section; 'with' anticipates ἔχοντες and the closing ellipsis marks the break. Nothing else supplied.
baehrens: PG 70; Fragmenta in Ezechielem frag rem mid

title: The Shepherd and the Water
english: …and fine, clear water, namely the instruction given through Moses, which was well able to guide them to the truth, in a way trampled the pasture and muddied the water as well (Ezekiel 34:18), setting a thick, material teaching, full of earthly impurity, before those who followed them as sheep follow rams.

“And I will raise up over them one shepherd … my servant David” (Ezekiel 34:23). That he says such things about Christ is easy to see. For when the blessed David had already died and was already lying in the tomb, the blessed Ezekiel prophesied; and God the Father made the promise as one that would come to pass in due time, not as one already fulfilled. For promises concern what is yet to be, not what has already been done.
translator_notes: Copy-text: PG 70, Fragmenta in Ezechielem (Greek), via the Khazarzar transcription.

Opens mid-sentence, finishing the clause begun at the end of the previous section ('and with, as it were, the finest pasture…'); the leading ellipsis marks the join. The Levites are the subject: they have the pasture and the water, which is the instruction given through Moses, and they trample and muddy it.
οὐκ ἀνικάνως ἔχουσαν is litotes ('not unable'); rendered 'well able'.
παρατιθέντες διδασκαλίαν: 'setting a teaching before' the flock; the teaching is what is thick, material and full of earthly impurity.
τοῖς ἐν τάξει προβάτων ἀκολουθοῦσιν αὐτοῖς ὡς κριοῖς: those who follow them as sheep follow rams. The rams may echo Ezekiel 34:17 (κριῶν), but that is uncertain and left uncited.
The trampled pasture and muddied water take up Ezekiel 34:18 (κατεπατεῖτε ... ἐταράσσετε).
The lemma is Ezekiel 34:23 LXX (ἀναστήσω ἐπ' αὐτοὺς ποιμένα ἕνα ... τὸν δοῦλόν μου Δαυιδ); the catena's own ellipsis is kept.
ἀταλαίπωρον ἰδεῖν: 'easy to see'.
προεφήτευσε μέν ... Ἐποιεῖτο δέ: the pair joins Ezekiel's prophecy with the Father's promise; ὁ Θεὸς καὶ Πατήρ is rendered 'God the Father'.
Catena reference Cat. f. 225 and the stray page number at the end of the printed text are dropped from the reading text.
baehrens: PG 70; Fragmenta in Ezechielem frag rem close
